Estimation of simple SBMs with missing data

Source: R/estimateMissSBM.R
estimateMissSBM.Rd

Variational EM inference of Stochastic Block Models indexed by block number from a partially observed network.

Usage

estimateMissSBM(
  adjacencyMatrix,
  vBlocks,
  sampling,
  covariates = list(),
  control = missSBM_param()
)

Arguments

adjacencyMatrix

The N x N adjacency matrix of the network data. If adjacencyMatrix is symmetric, we assume an undirected network with no loop; otherwise the network is assumed to be directed.

vBlocks

The vector of number of blocks considered in the collection.

sampling

The sampling design, the model of the process that originates the missing data: MAR designs ("dyad", "node", "covar-dyad", "covar-node", "snowball") and MNAR designs ("double-standard", "block-dyad", "block-node", "degree") are available. See details.

covariates

An optional list with M entries (the M covariates). If the covariates are node-centered, each entry of covariates must be a size-N vector; if the covariates are dyad-centered, each entry of covariates must be N x N matrix.

control

a list-like structure for controlling advanced features, with default generated by missSBM_param. See the associated documentation for details.

Value

Returns an R6 object with class missSBM_collection.

Details

Internal functions use future_lapply, so set your plan to 'multisession' or 'multicore' to use several cores/workers.

The sampling designs are either Missing At Random (MAR) or Missing Not At Random (MNAR), and observe either dyads or nodes (all the dyads of an observed node). See doi:10.1080/01621459.2018.1562934 for a complete description. The parameters of each design:

  • Missing At Random (MAR)

    • "dyad": p, the probability that a dyad is observed.

    • "node": p, the probability that a node is observed.

    • "covar-dyad": \(\beta \in R^M\), a dyad (i, j) being observed with probability \(logistic(\beta' x_{ij})\), \(x_{ij}\) the covariates of the dyad.

    • "covar-node": \(\beta \in R^M\), a node i being observed with probability \(logistic(\beta' x_i)\), \(x_i\) the covariates of the node.

    • "snowball": (number of waves, proportion of the nodes observed in the first wave); the nodes of each wave are the neighbors of the nodes of the previous one. It is fitted as "node" sampling.

  • Missing Not At Random (MNAR)

    • "double-standard": (p0, p1), the probabilities that a dyad is observed if it is 0 and if it is 1. (p0, p1) are identified through the differences of connectivity between the blocks: with a single block, they are not identifiable, and the model is fitted with p0 = p1, i.e. as dyad sampling (with a warning).

    • "block-node": \((p_1, \dots, p_Q)\), \(p_q\) the probability that a node of block q is observed.

    • "block-dyad": the Q x Q matrix \((p_{ql})\), \(p_{ql}\) the probability that a dyad between blocks q and l is observed.

    • "degree": (a, b), a node i being observed with probability \(logistic(a + b D_i)\), \(D_i\) its degree.

The number of blocks is selected by the ICL (Integrated Classification Likelihood, the smaller the better): -2 times the variational lower bound of the log-likelihood of the observed data (the observed dyads and the sampling matrix), at the MAP memberships, plus a penalty, in which the connectivity counts the observed dyads and the parameters of the sampling all the dyads (or all the nodes). The ICLs of different designs fitted to the same data can be compared to choose the design. When their samplings carry the same information (e.g. "block-node" and "degree" on an assortative network, where the degree depends on the block), the ICLs differ by a few units, about the penalty of one parameter (log N), and the partitions are the same: such a difference is no evidence for one design. Each number of blocks is fitted from a spectral clustering, then improved by a polish and by passes of exploration splitting and merging blocks (see missSBM_param); one pass is enough on small networks, two are advised for a reference analysis of a network with many blocks.

See also

observeNetwork, missSBM_collection, missSBM_fit and missSBM_param.

Examples

## SBM parameters
N <- 100 # number of nodes
Q <- 3   # number of blocks
pi <- rep(1,Q)/Q     # block proportion
theta <- list(mean = diag(.45,Q) + .05 ) # connectivity matrix

## Sampling parameters
samplingParameters <- .75 # the sampling rate
sampling  <- "dyad"      # the sampling design

## generate an undirected binary SBM with no covariate
sbm <- sbm::sampleSimpleSBM(N, pi, theta)

## Uncomment to set parallel computing with future
## future::plan("multicore", workers = 2)

## Sample some dyads data + Infer SBM with missing data
collection <-
   observeNetwork(sbm$networkData, sampling, samplingParameters) %>%
   estimateMissSBM(vBlocks = 1:4, sampling = sampling)
#> 
#> 
#>  Adjusting Variational EM for Stochastic Block Model
#> 
#> 	Imputation assumes a 'dyad' network-sampling process
#> 
#>  Initialization of 4 model(s). 
#>  Performing VEM inference
#>  	Model with 4 blocks.
 	Model with 3 blocks.
 	Model with 2 blocks.
 	Model with 1 blocks.
 Polishing (node-swap)
#> 
#>  Looking for better solutions
#>  Pass 1   Going forward +++
                                                                                                    
 Pass 1   Going backward +++
                                                                                                    

plot(collection, "monitoring")

plot(collection, "icl")


collection$ICL
#> [1] 9283.987 8785.037 8566.070 8606.452
coef(collection$bestModel$fittedSBM, "connectivity")
#> $mean
#>            [,1]       [,2]       [,3]
#> [1,] 0.49037793 0.05779239 0.03823879
#> [2,] 0.05779239 0.47647349 0.05993739
#> [3,] 0.03823879 0.05993739 0.50684957
#> 

myModel <- collection$bestModel
plot(myModel, "expected")

plot(myModel, "imputed")

plot(myModel, "meso")
coef(myModel, "sampling")
#> [1] 0.7519192
coef(myModel, "connectivity")
#> $mean
#>            [,1]       [,2]       [,3]
#> [1,] 0.49037793 0.05779239 0.03823879
#> [2,] 0.05779239 0.47647349 0.05993739
#> [3,] 0.03823879 0.05993739 0.50684957
#> 
predict(myModel)[1:5, 1:5]
